prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

Anyone who begins a sentence with, “In all honesty ... ” is about to tell a lie. Anyone who says, “This is how I feel” had better love form more than disclosure. Same for anyone who thinks he thinks well because he had a thought. If you say, “You’re ugly” to an ugly person — no credit for honesty, which must always be a discovery, an act that qualifies as an achievement. If you persist you’re just a cruel bastard, a pig without a mirror, somebody who hasn’t examined himself enough. A hesitation hints at an attempt to be honest, suggests a difficulty is present. A good sentence needs a clause or two, interruptions, set off by commas, evidence of a slowing down, a rethinking. Before I asked my wife to marry me, I told her I’d never be fully honest. No one, she said, had ever said that to her. I was trying to be radically honest, I said, but in fact had another motive. A claim without a “but” in it is, at best, only half true. In all honesty, I was asking in advance to be forgiven.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- People who announce their honesty often signal that they are about to be dishonest.
- True honesty is not merely blunt disclosure but a difficult achievement that requires self-examination.
- Cruel remarks should not be mistaken for honesty when they reveal no insight or discovery.
- Hesitation, complexity, and revision in speech can indicate a more genuine attempt at honesty.
- The narrator admits that his claim of radical honesty before proposing was partly a request for future forgiveness.

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Anyone, This, Same

outputs.L1:
Anyone who begins a sentence with “In all honesty . . .” is likely preparing to lie. Anyone who says, “This is how I feel,” had better love form more than disclosure. The same is true of anyone who thinks he thinks well simply because he has had a thought. If you say, “You’re ugly,” to an ugly person, you deserve no credit for honesty, which must always be a discovery—an act worthy of being called an achievement. If you persist, you are merely a cruel bastard, a pig without a mirror, someone who has not examined himself closely enough.

A hesitation suggests an attempt at honesty; it signals that some difficulty is present. A good sentence needs a clause or two, interruptions set off by commas, evidence of slowing down, of reconsideration. Before I asked my wife to marry me, I told her I would never be fully honest. No one, she said, had ever said that to her. I told her I was trying to be radically honest, though in fact I had another motive. A claim without a “but” in it is, at best, only half true. In all honesty, I was asking, in advance, to be forgiven.
outputs.L2:
People who open with “To be perfectly honest…” are usually preparing to deceive you. People who announce, “That’s just what I feel,” should care more about shaping the statement than merely revealing themselves. The same applies to someone who mistakes having a thought for thinking intelligently.

Calling an unattractive person ugly earns no praise for truthfulness. Honesty has to uncover something; it has to be an accomplishment. Keep doing it and you are simply vicious—a swine lacking a mirror, someone who has not looked closely enough at himself.

A pause can signal a real effort at honesty; it implies that something difficult is being worked through. A strong sentence often requires a couple of clauses, some interruptions, commas that show the mind slowing, reconsidering.

Before proposing to my wife, I told her I would never be completely truthful. She said no one had ever told her that before. I said I was attempting a kind of extreme honesty, though I actually had another reason. Any assertion that contains no “but” is, at best, only partly true. To be perfectly honest, I was asking ahead of time to be pardoned.
outputs.L3:
People who make a point of announcing their honesty often deserve to be treated with caution. Phrases such as “I’m just being honest” or “to tell you the truth” can sometimes function less as proof of sincerity than as a warning that something else is going on. They may be used to excuse cruelty, to prepare the listener for a self-serving confession, or to give moral cover to words that are careless, manipulative, or incomplete. The declaration of honesty can become a performance: a way of claiming virtue before the truth has actually been tested.

True honesty is more difficult than blunt disclosure. It is not simply saying whatever comes first to mind, nor is it the same as exposing every harsh opinion one happens to hold. Genuine honesty requires self-examination. It asks a person to look closely at their motives, their fears, their evasions, and the ways they may be deceiving themselves before they speak to someone else. A person can reveal a fact and still be dishonest about its meaning. Likewise, a person can speak plainly and still be avoiding the deeper truth.

For that reason, cruelty should not be confused with honesty. A cutting remark is not necessarily brave or truthful simply because it is unpleasant. If it reveals no real insight, if it costs the speaker nothing, and if it is aimed only at wounding another person, then it may be merely aggression disguised as candor. Honesty should involve some kind of discovery—about the situation, about the other person, or about oneself. Without that discovery, the claim of honesty becomes thin and suspect.

In fact, the more genuine attempt at honesty may appear less confident on the surface. Hesitation, complexity, qualification, and revision can all suggest that a speaker is struggling to say something accurately rather than merely forcefully. Someone who pauses, corrects themselves, or admits uncertainty may be closer to the truth than someone who delivers a cruel judgment with absolute certainty. Honest speech often has to make room for contradiction, shame, confusion, and the possibility that one’s first version of events was incomplete.

The narrator recognizes this problem in his own past. When he claimed a commitment to radical honesty before proposing, he presented it as a noble principle, as though he were offering a relationship built on complete truthfulness. But he later admits that this claim was not entirely pure. It was also, in part, a request for future forgiveness. By announcing his honesty in advance, he was preparing a defense for whatever pain his future confessions might cause. His supposed openness contained a hidden bargain: he wanted to be admired for telling the truth and forgiven for the damage that truth might do. In acknowledging this, he shows that honesty is not a simple possession but a difficult and ongoing effort to understand what one is really saying, and why.
outputs.L4:
Honesty is often spoken of as though it were simple: a clear choice between telling the truth and telling a lie, between being sincere and being false. Yet the more closely we examine honesty, the less simple it becomes. To say “I am honest” may already be to simplify oneself too much, to overlook all the hidden motives, evasions, fears, and half-truths that accompany even our most sincere declarations. Honesty is not merely the absence of lying. It is a difficult and often uncomfortable discipline of looking at oneself without flattery.

A person may tell the truth and still deceive. One may state the facts accurately while concealing the reason for stating them. One may confess something in order to appear noble, remain silent in order to avoid cruelty, or exaggerate one’s sincerity in order to gain trust. Even the claim “I only want to be honest” can be suspicious. It may mean: I want to hurt you without being blamed. It may mean: I want to relieve myself of guilt. It may mean: I want you to forgive me in advance for what I am about to say. Honesty, then, is not a pure possession. It is a struggle with oneself.

This is why aphorisms about truth often sound paradoxical. The person who loudly insists on his truthfulness may be the one most in need of doubt. The person who hesitates, qualifies, and revises may be closer to honesty than the person who speaks with absolute certainty. A completely confident declaration of sincerity can become a form of self-deception, because the self is never entirely transparent to itself. We do not always know why we act. We do not always know what we want. We often discover our motives only after we have already spoken in their name.

A personal anecdote makes this problem clearer. Imagine a man reflecting on the moment he proposed marriage. If he said, “I was completely honest when I asked her to marry me,” the statement might seem admirable at first. But was he entirely honest? Did he know everything that was contained in that proposal? Perhaps he loved her deeply, but perhaps he also feared loneliness. Perhaps he desired commitment, but perhaps he also desired security, admiration, or escape from uncertainty. Perhaps he believed every word he said, and yet did not fully understand what those words would demand of him in the future.

The proposal may have been sincere, but sincerity does not guarantee complete truth. At such a moment, a person speaks not only from knowledge but also from hope. He promises a future self he has not yet become. He says “always” without knowing what years will do to him. He says “I love you” with real feeling, but that feeling is mixed with imagination, desire, fear, pride, and expectation. To call the moment simply honest would be to erase its complexity. To call it dishonest would also be unjust. The truth lies somewhere more difficult: he meant what he said, but he did not fully know what he meant.

This is the central difficulty of honesty. It is not enough to avoid deliberate falsehood. One must also be willing to question the comfort of one’s own explanations. Real honesty requires hesitation. It requires the ability to say, “This is what I believe, though I may be hiding something from myself.” It requires the courage to admit that our motives are mixed and that our words often outrun our understanding. Honest speech is therefore rarely absolute. It is careful, provisional, and aware of its own limits.

For that reason, the proud statement “I am honest” is never complete. At best, it is an aspiration. At worst, it is a disguise. It may conceal vanity, aggression, or a desire to be excused. Many declarations of honesty are really pleas for forgiveness: forgive me for my bluntness, forgive me for my weakness, forgive me for not knowing myself better, forgive me for the harm I may do while claiming to tell the truth. The honest person is not the one who claims perfect honesty, but the one who remains suspicious of that claim.

True honesty, then, is not a possession one can announce once and for all. It is a practice of self-scrutiny, a willingness to pause before speaking, and a recognition that truth is often entangled with uncertainty. To be honest is not to be simple. It is to accept complexity without using it as an excuse. It is to speak as truthfully as one can while remembering that even one’s truthfulness may be incomplete.
outputs.L5:
Anyone can make a difference in the world, no matter where they come from or what challenges they face. This simple truth reminds us that every action, even a small one, can have meaning. A kind word, a helpful gesture, or a moment of patience can change someone’s day.

At the same time, we are all connected by many of the same hopes and needs. We want respect, understanding, safety, and happiness. When we remember this, it becomes easier to treat others with compassion. Although people may live different lives, the same basic feelings unite us all.

This is why kindness matters. Anyone can choose to be kind, and that choice can create a better world for everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a short literary essay in a sharp, aphoristic style about the phrase “In all honesty” and why honesty is more complicated than blunt truth-telling.
counterfactuals.output:
“In all honesty” is a curious phrase because it announces the very thing it asks us not to doubt. It is a lantern lit at noon, a signature beneath a face. The words suggest that honesty is not our native weather but a special climate into which we must momentarily step.

Blunt truth-telling is often mistaken for honesty because it has the glamour of violence. It strikes quickly, leaves evidence, and congratulates itself on refusing ornament. But a hammer is not more honest than a hand because it is harder. To tell the truth without tact may be less an act of courage than a failure of imagination. The blunt person says, “I only tell it like it is,” as if reality were a stone and not also a wound, a memory, a timing, a listener.

Honesty is not merely the absence of lying. It is the discipline of proportion. It asks not only, “Is this true?” but “What truth is this serving?” A fact can be accurate and still be false to the moment. One may describe the weather at a funeral and say nothing untrue, yet say nothing honest. Honesty requires attention to the whole human scene: motive, consequence, mercy, fear.

The phrase “In all honesty” often appears just before a confession, a criticism, or a betrayal. It is a small ceremonial clearing of the throat before the knife enters. Yet it can also be an act of humility: an admission that speech is compromised, that even sincerity needs a preface. We say it because we know language is slippery, because we know we have edited ourselves, because we know truth arrives dressed in temperament.

Honesty, then, is not the same as exposure. It is not flinging open every door in the house. Some rooms are private; some are not yet ready for light. The honest person is not the one who says everything, but the one who does not make a god of concealment or of disclosure. Silence can be cowardice; it can also be care.

“In all honesty” is less a guarantee than a plea. It asks to be believed while admitting belief is fragile. The phrase reminds us that truth is not a weapon we possess but a responsibility we enter. To be honest is not simply to be blunt. It is to speak in such a way that reality, however difficult, is not diminished by cruelty, vanity, or haste.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a first-person prose poem about honesty, cruelty, marriage, and the ways people use sincerity as an excuse.
counterfactuals.output:
I have learned that honesty can arrive with clean hands and still leave blood on the table. I have seen it dressed for church, seated upright at dinner, saying, I only tell the truth, as if truth were a license and not a blade. In marriage, we called this intimacy: the unlocked door, the uncurtained window, the sentence beginning with don’t be angry but. We mistook exposure for devotion. We stood in the kitchen under the humming light and offered each other our worst thoughts like dowries.

I said I was being sincere when I named the parts of you I could not love. You said you were being honest when you held my failures to the mirror until they trembled. We both believed cruelty became sacred if we refused to soften it. How proud we were of our sharpness. How faithful to the wound.

But truth is not the same as confession, and confession is not the same as care. A fact can be thrown. A feeling can be sharpened. There are people who strip themselves naked just to make others cold, who call it bravery when they mean appetite, who say, This is who I am, and wait to be congratulated for not becoming kinder.

I am trying now to tell the truth without making a weapon of it. I am trying to love without demanding applause for my restraint. In the ruins of my own candor, I kneel and gather what I once called honesty: every stone I hurled, every window I broke just to prove there was glass.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a paragraph in the style of a contemporary essayist, full of paradoxes and self-corrections, exploring the idea that real honesty requires hesitation and form.
counterfactuals.output: Real honesty, if it is real—though the word “real” already begins to flatter itself—does not arrive naked, as we like to pretend, but dressed, delayed, awkwardly buttoned into form. The blunt person is often not honest so much as impatient; he has mistaken speed for purity, injury for truth. To say what one means is not to say the first thing one feels, since feeling, that little tyrant, is frequently only weather passing through the body. Honesty requires hesitation: the pause in which one discovers that the truth has more than one face, or that one’s bravest confession is partly vanity, or that silence, too, can be a kind of lie—unless it is mercy, unless it is fear, unless it is simply the only shape the truth can bear for now. Form is not the enemy of sincerity but its discipline, the glass that lets water be held. Without it, candor spills everywhere and calls the flooding virtue. I distrust the polished sentence, of course; it can conceal as much as reveal. But I distrust even more the sentence that claims not to be polished, that throws itself on the table and says, “Here, this is me,” when it is only another costume, the costume of having no costume. Perhaps honesty is never the absence of artifice, but the ethical use of it: a stammer arranged carefully enough to remain a stammer, a truth slowed down until it can stop performing and begin, at last, to answer for itself.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a brief, intimate monologue that begins by criticizing people who announce their honesty and ends with a confession about proposing to one’s wife.
counterfactuals.output:
People who announce their honesty always make me nervous. “To be honest,” they say, as if truth is a coat they put on for company, as if the rest of the time they’ve been walking around in costume.

I’ve never trusted that. Real honesty is quieter. It sits at the edge of the bed after an argument. It washes a glass it didn’t use. It says, “I was afraid,” when it would be easier to say, “I was tired.”

And I have been afraid. Of being known too well. Of being forgiven and still not changing. Of loving someone so much that my whole life could be measured by the sound of her keys in the door.

So here’s the truth, without a trumpet: I didn’t propose to my wife because I was certain. I proposed because I finally understood I wanted to be uncertain with her for the rest of my life.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a dense, witty meditation on truthfulness where the narrator argues that any claim without a “but” is only half true.
counterfactuals.output:
A sentence without a “but” is a room without a window: admirable in its firmness, useful for storage, and almost certainly unfit for human habitation.

I do not distrust truth. I distrust truth arriving without luggage. The honest fact comes scuffed, delayed, carrying contrary evidence in one hand and an apology in the other. “I love you” is true, but I am tired. “He is guilty,” but so are the circumstances that trained his hands. “This is progress,” but listen for what it crushes under its clean new wheels. “I was right,” but not as right as I needed to be, nor as wrong as my enemies hoped.

The “but” is not the enemy of truth. It is truth’s hinge. Without it, assertions become monuments, and monuments, as a rule, are erected just when the living have become inconvenient. A claim that cannot bend will eventually break, or worse, be used as a club by someone delighted to discover it has no moving parts.

Of course, there are people who despise the “but.” They call it weakness, relativism, evasion, a fog machine rented by cowards. These people prefer their truths boneless and bright, like pills. They want declarations with the nutritional profile of thunder: loud, immediate, and gone. They say, “Facts don’t care about your feelings,” but facts, if they are facts, must care about everything relevant, including the feeling that caused the witness to lie, the fear that edited the memory, the grief that made a statistic out of a son.

Even arithmetic, that severe little monastery, has its cloisters of qualification. Two and two make four, but only once we have agreed what “two,” “and,” “make,” and “four” are doing in the sentence. The universe itself, which seems at first to speak in absolutes, mutters footnotes at every scale. Light is a wave, but also a particle. Matter is solid, but mostly space. Time is steady, but ask a clock on a mountain, ask a twin in a rocket, ask anyone waiting for a diagnosis.

The “but” is where intelligence draws breath. It is the mind refusing to be stamped into slogan. It does not cancel the first half of the sentence; it civilizes it. It says: continue. It says: the world is not finished merely because you have described one corner of it. It says: beware the period that arrives too early dressed as certainty.

This is why liars often sound so pure. They have sanded off all the buts. Their stories gleam with a cleanliness only fraud can afford. The truthful person hesitates, revises, complicates, irritates. He brings receipts, but also context; confesses error, but not collapse; grants the opponent a point, but not the kingdom. He is less quotable than the fanatic and less soothing than the fool, which is why he is rarely invited to dinner until after the disaster.

Still, one must not worship the “but” blindly. There is a cowardly “but,” a perfumed trapdoor through which responsibility escapes: “I’m sorry, but…” “I didn’t mean to, but…” “I believe in justice, but…” The wicked know the hinge too; they oil it with sophistication. A good “but” enlarges truth. A bad one evicts it.

So perhaps my rule needs its own correction, as all decent rules do. Any claim without a “but” is only half true, but any claim with too many is afraid to be true at all. The art lies in knowing where the hinge belongs: not so early that the door never opens, not so late that everyone has suffocated inside.

Truthfulness, then, is not the recital of clean propositions. It is the discipline of keeping faith with the whole sentence. It is saying what is so, but also what resists it; what we know, but also what we are paid not to notice; what we hope, but also what hope has no right to erase.

I want a language with joints. I want convictions that can kneel without surrendering. I want the kind of honesty that does not mistake bluntness for courage or nuance for retreat. Give me the sentence that walks with a limp and reaches the end alive.

The world is simple, but not for long.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
